name: Tomas Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the guitar players for a small opera theatre, record guide parts for singers and teach five pupils at a music school. I have a music master’s and the director trusts my ear, but our contracts pay a typical musician wage. I like finding the exact quiet chord that lets a voice come forward.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that schedule ask of your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a clinic nurse with rotating shifts, so our two school-age children’s pickup needs a calendar of its own. We have a mortgage and about three months saved. There are some similar posts nearby, but carrying a guitar to an audition is not the same as holding a new paid contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the singers that quicker email replies are fine if the paid rehearsal stays on the sheet. A guitar part still has to follow a human breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have three months of expenses saved and my partner’s clinic wages are fairly steady. A cancelled guide part would be annoying, though a whole missing opera week would make the mortgage tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid opera rehearsals and five music-school pupils this season. I use AI now and then to sort booking messages, checking each call against the stage manager’s sheet; before next season I would request the cancellation fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about irregular show dates. A plateau in AI leaves those ordinary contract gaps on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a call sheet save you trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rehearsal moved one hour earlier last winter, and the email still had the old time. I checked the signed sheet before arranging pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for after a cancellation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the theatre for half the rehearsal fee if it cancels late. The mortgage does not shift because an opera runs short.

say: I would accept **faster emails** while keeping rehearsal fees written.
I would request a **late cancellation fee** next season.
think: Our **three-month reserve** handles a small missed guide fee.
A whole **lost opera week** would still strain the mortgage.
do: Keep **paid opera rehearsals** and five music-school pupils this season.
Request a **written half-fee term** before next season.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about ordinary changes to paid show dates.
S0.quote: The mortgage does not shift because an opera runs short.
fieldNote: His **senior ear** earns typical musician pay with three months saved and partner clinic wages.
He checks occasional **AI booking help** against the signed call sheet.

steps.text: Keep paid opera rehearsals and five music-school pupils this season
Request written half-fee term for late theatre cancellation before next season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the company that cheap generated guide parts could remove hours from our invoices. I would ask the musicians’ association for a fee when a recording is reused, not just when we play it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The singer guides are about a quarter of my own pay and may lose buyers. Live opera still needs players now, but shorter contracts would make the three-month reserve feel thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the association to compare our guide invoices and ask the theatre engineer to show me its new AI cue aligner, a tool that checks where a recorded cue meets the stage call. In the first year I would test it only on a guitar file I own after the engineer confirms a free trial, compare every marked entry with the original recording and live call, and stop if it shifts a note or sends the file outside the theatre server.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a sustained guide-fee cut. Learning one tool gives me some control, but the theatre still has to pay for my part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try it on a pupil’s audio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would leave pupil recordings out of the trial. The engineer can demonstrate it on my own take without asking a family to accept a new storage rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association put on the invoice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a separate preparation line and a reuse line. A recording played every week should not be paid once and forgotten.

say: I would seek **preparation and reuse fees** through the association.
I would tell singers that **generated guides** could remove paid hours.
think: Singer **guide parts** provide about a quarter of my pay.
A shorter **opera contract** would make three months of savings feel thin.
do: Bring **guide invoices** to the association for preparation and reuse terms this month.
Test the **cue aligner** after engineer instruction on owned audio and free trial; compare original/live call, stop on errors or leakage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about guide fees and possible shorter live contracts.
S1.quote: A recording played every week should not be paid once and forgotten.
fieldNote: His **new tool learning** goes beyond occasional AI booking and uses an engineer-led free trial.
Owned **guitar audio** stays on theatre servers, with manual checks against original and live call.

steps.text: Ask musicians’ association for paid preparation and reuse terms this month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI could make a singer's guide track before breakfast in 2028. Hands-on playing robots arrive around 2031, three years later, but the guide fees can go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the singer guides to stop selling in 2028, roughly a quarter of my pay. The theatre may also shorten the season, and I cannot count on my partner’s shifts to replace either stream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for signed paid opera dates and count guide invoices with my partner. In the first year after 2028, if guide orders stop and paid shows fall, I would apply for a posted school guitar-coordinator job only if it accepts my master’s and any required teaching licence I hold, written net pay after travel and childcare beats the lost fees, and pickup fits; I would keep the opera and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the expected guide loss, with three months saved and some local posts giving us a search window. If paid opera weeks also collapse, I would be alarmed, but that is not certain yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new licence before seeing a post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the posted requirement first. I would not buy a course for a vacancy that might accept my present degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner cover the school audition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the clinic roster confirms an early shift that week. A regular new job would need its own pickup plan.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 playing robots.
I would request **signed paid opera dates** now.
think: I expect **guide fees** to vanish before robots reach the stage.
A larger **opera cut** remains possible, not certain.
do: Request **signed opera dates** and count guide invoices this week.
Seek **posted school work** only if 2028 guides and shows fall, qualified, written net pay beats losses after travel/childcare and pickup fits.
Keep **opera and pupils** until a suitable written school offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected guide loss while show cuts remain uncertain.
S2.quote: Thinking AGI could make a singer's guide track before breakfast in 2028.
fieldNote: The **2028 guide loss** precedes possible 2031 robotic playing and removes about a quarter of his own music pay.
The school role needs **posted eligibility**, written net replacement pay, pickup and a signed offer.

steps.text: Seek eligible posted school role if 2028 guides and shows fall; replacement written net-after-travel/childcare, pickup
Keep paid opera and five pupils until suitable written school offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the singers that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to prove a live guitar class can earn. Robots able to play follow around 2034, after software changes guide tracks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide fees might vanish in 2031. A separate adult accompaniment class could replace some money if it pays for my preparation, not just the hour in front of the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next autumn I would ask the independent civic hall for a room after our children’s pickup. I would run a six-week adult accompaniment class only if seven people prepay enough to cover room hire, my teaching and preparation, and the hall checks amplifier cables or students bring safe acoustic guitars; in the first year after 2031 I would repeat it only if seven still prepay room and my time, the room remains available after pickup and instruments stay safe. I would keep paid opera calls meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until seven people actually pay. Five years before AGI lets me test a paid accompaniment class without using mortgage savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check a cable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall technician would check outlets and amplifier cables before anyone plugs in. If that is not possible, we use acoustic guitars in good order or cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four adults pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees will not pay room hire or my preparation. I would refund them and keep my regular school pupils.

say: I would offer a **paid accompaniment class** with real prepayments.
I would cancel if **four fees** cannot cover room and preparation.
think: The **guide fees** may end in 2031 before 2034 robots.
Seven **prepaid places** must fund room, teaching and preparation.
do: Start **adult guitar class** only with seven prepayments covering room, teaching/preparation, pickup fit, and checked cables or safe acoustic guitars.
Renew **paid class** after 2031 only with seven prepayments covering room and time, available room after pickup and safe equipment.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the independent class pays for preparation.
S3.quote: Five years before AGI lets me test a paid accompaniment class without using mortgage savings.
fieldNote: A separate **guitar class** requires seven prepayments paying room hire, teaching and preparation.
The hall checks **electrical cables** or adults use safe acoustic guitars, with child pickup covered.

steps.text: Start class if seven prepay room/teaching/prep, pickup fits, cables checked or acoustic guitars safe
Renew class after 2031 if seven prepay room/time, room available after pickup and equipment safe
Keep paid opera calls while booked
Refund four prepayments rather than teach without covered room and preparation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that a decade until AGI by 2036 gives us time to learn work and ask who pays for it. Robots that can play guitars arrive around 2039, after thinking software changes the guide trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still be leading the guitar players, but the mortgage is due now. Three months saved gives us some room to plan, not a guarantee that every future opera contract stays paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save a fifth of each extra paid guide fee after food and mortgage until our reserve reaches six months. Through the decade I would continue the independent class only while seven adults prepay room, teaching and preparation, the room is available after pickup and equipment is safe; in the first year after 2036, if opera dates shrink, I would seek a posted school music-coordinator opening only if my qualifications are accepted, written net pay after travel and childcare replaces lost fees and pickup fits. I would keep opera and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the long-run contract. The current season is paid, so I can prepare without telling the children we are losing the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if guide fees stop before the reserve reaches six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save from spare paid lessons only after bills, while keeping two months untouched. A promised guide fee is not cash I can put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the theatre for a school title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a posted opening, written hours and net pay that improves our household position. I would keep the signed show calls until the school signs an offer.

I would separate **2036 thinking AGI** from 2039 playing robots.
think: The **mortgage** is due before AGI arrives.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because guide fees could stop before the theatre knows its next season. Signed paid opera dates, association reuse terms and a posted school role with accepted qualifications, written net pay and workable pickup would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who listens to the guitar part before a singer tries to learn it. A guide recording can be cheap and still cost a singer an afternoon if the chord is wrong.

headlineQuote: A guide recording can be cheap and still cost a singer an afternoon if the chord is wrong.
portrait: At **43**, Tomas leads opera guitar players with a music master’s and strong skill, records singer guides and teaches five pupils.
His **typical musician pay**, clinic-shift partner, mortgage, two children and three-month reserve make contract gaps matter.
He uses **AI occasionally** for booking and trials a new cue aligner only on owned audio with engineer instruction and manual checks.
He considers a **paid adult class** only with seven prepayments covering room, teaching and preparation, safe equipment and pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end singer-guide fees before the opera confirms paid dates.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed opera dates**, association reuse terms and an eligible posted school opening with written net pay and pickup would help.
